overview:
In Jain philosophy, the distinction between Arihant (also spelled Arhat or Arihanta) and Siddha is central to understanding the path and goal of liberation. Both terms refer to liberated or perfectly pure souls, yet they designate two different stages or conditions of that liberation.

An Arihant is a living, embodied omniscient being who has destroyed all ghātiyā karmas—the four destructive types of karma that obscure right knowledge, right perception, power, and bliss. Having attained kevalajñāna (omniscience) while still associated with a physical body, the Arihant remains present within the worldly realm (saṃsāra) until the non‑destructive aghātiyā karmas—those determining body, lifespan, status, and feeling—are exhausted. In many contexts, especially in lay devotion, the term Arihant is closely associated with Tīrthaṅkaras, the ford‑makers who establish or re‑establish the Jain community and its teachings in a given time cycle. However, technically, any kevalin who has destroyed the ghātiyā karmas is an Arihant, whether or not they function as a Tīrthaṅkara.

A Siddha, by contrast, is a soul that has completely transcended all karmic bondage, both destructive and non‑destructive. Upon the final shedding of the remaining aghātiyā karmas at the moment of death of an Arihant or any kevalin, the soul rises to the top of the universe (loka), the Siddhaśilā, and abides there eternally as a disembodied, pure consciousness. Siddhas are characterized by infinite knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy, but they no longer act, teach, or intervene in the world. They are the perfected ideal, the ultimate goal toward which all Jain spiritual practice is directed.

From the perspective of the Jain ontological scheme (tattvas), both Arihant and Siddha are liberated beings, yet the Arihant is still within the realm of motion and time, while the Siddha is beyond all change. The Arihant’s presence in the world allows for the direct preaching of the dharma and the establishment of a fourfold community of monks, nuns, laymen, and laywomen. The Siddha, on the other hand, is a silent exemplar of perfection, serving as the ultimate object of contemplation and aspiration rather than a living teacher.

In terms of the stages of spiritual development (guṇasthāna), the Arihant corresponds to the highest embodied stages, particularly the 13th and 14th guṇasthānas, where all ghātiyā karmas have been destroyed and omniscience is attained. The transition from Arihant to Siddha occurs at the moment of final bodily death, when the last remnants of aghātiyā karma fall away. Thus, the distinction is not one of qualitative difference in purity of consciousness—both are perfectly pure—but of existential condition: embodied versus disembodied, within saṃsāra versus beyond it.

Devotional practice reflects this distinction through the Navakāra (Namaskāra) Mantra, in which Arihants and Siddhas are praised separately: “Ṇamo Arihantāṇaṃ” (I bow to the Arihants) and “Ṇamo Siddhāṇaṃ” (I bow to the Siddhas). The separate invocations underscore that Arihants are revered as present teachers and ford‑makers, while Siddhas are honored as the consummation of the spiritual path. Philosophically, this dual focus helps practitioners keep in view both the living guidance of enlightened beings and the ultimate, bodiless state of liberation.

Across Jain traditions—Digambara and Śvetāmbara—the basic doctrinal distinction between Arihant and Siddha is shared, though details of cosmology, enumeration of Tīrthaṅkaras, and narrative traditions may differ. Scholastic texts systematize this distinction in terms of karma theory, cosmology, and epistemology, while devotional and ethical literature emphasizes the Arihant’s compassion and teaching activity and the Siddha’s perfect, immutable bliss. Together, the concepts of Arihant and Siddha articulate a dynamic vision of liberation: a path that culminates in omniscience within the world and then in eternal, bodiless perfection beyond it.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra
primary_sources.author: Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmin
primary_sources.translation:
When all karmas are exhausted, the soul is a Siddha.
When the destructive karmas are destroyed, the soul is an Arihant.
primary_sources.notes: The Tattvārthasūtra is a foundational Jain philosophical text accepted by both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions. In its chapters on karma and liberation, it distinguishes the state in which ghātiyā karmas are destroyed (yielding an embodied omniscient being, Arihant) from the final state in which all karmas, including aghātiyā, are exhausted (yielding a Siddha). The brief aphoristic style requires commentary, but these sutras are often cited to explain the technical difference between Arihant and Siddha.

primary_sources.title: Sarvārthasiddhi (Commentary on Tattvārthasūtra)
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Pūjyapāda
primary_sources.original_text: घातिकर्मक्षयेऽर्हन्निर्दोषज्ञानदर्शनादिगुणसम्पन्नो देहवान्। सर्वकर्मक्षये तु देहादिव्यवच्छेदेन सिद्धो नाम।
primary_sources.transliteration:
ghātikarmakṣaye'rhannirdoṣajñānadarśanādiguṇasampanno dehavān.
sarvakarmakṣaye tu dehādivyavacchedena siddho nāma.
primary_sources.translation: Upon the destruction of the destructive karmas, the Arihant, endowed with flawless knowledge, perception, and other qualities, still possesses a body. When all karmas are destroyed, then, through the cessation of body and the like, the soul is called a Siddha.
primary_sources.notes: Sarvārthasiddhi is a classical Digambara commentary that elaborates the terse sutras of Tattvārthasūtra. Here, Pūjyapāda explicitly defines Arihant as an embodied omniscient being and Siddha as a disembodied liberated soul, clarifying that the difference lies in the presence or absence of remaining non‑destructive karmas and the physical body.

primary_sources.title: Navakāra (Namaskāra) Mantra
primary_sources.author: Canonical Jain liturgical formula (author not individually specified)
primary_sources.translation:
I bow to the Arihants.
I bow to the Siddhas.
primary_sources.notes: The Navakāra Mantra is one of the most important Jain devotional recitations, honoring five categories of revered beings. The separate mention of Arihants and Siddhas reflects their distinct roles: Arihants as living, teaching omniscients and Siddhas as fully liberated, bodiless souls. This liturgical distinction reinforces the doctrinal differentiation found in philosophical texts.

primary_sources.title: Samayasāra
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Kundakunda
primary_sources.original_text:
अरिहंतो तु णाणदंसणचरित्तसुद्धो देहधारी।
सिद्धो तु देहविरहियो परमसुद्धो णिरंतरं सुखी।
primary_sources.transliteration:
arihanto tu ñāṇadaṃsaṇacarittasuddho dehadhārī.
siddho tu dehavirahiyo paramasuddho ṇiraṃtaraṃ sukhī.
primary_sources.translation:
The Arihant is pure in knowledge, perception, and conduct, yet still bears a body.
The Siddha, devoid of body, is supremely pure and continuously blissful.
primary_sources.notes: Samayasāra, a key Digambara text, focuses on the nature of the soul and its pure state. In verses like these, Kundakunda distinguishes Arihant and Siddha by emphasizing the Arihant’s embodied condition and the Siddha’s bodiless, eternally blissful state. The text is influential in technical discussions of the soul’s progression from embodied omniscience to final liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Arihant and Siddha are completely identical, with no meaningful distinction between them.
misconceptions.reality: While both Arihant and Siddha are perfectly pure souls, Jain doctrine clearly distinguishes them by existential condition. An Arihant is an omniscient, liberated being who still possesses a body and remains within the worldly realm until the exhaustion of non‑destructive karmas. A Siddha is a fully liberated, disembodied soul that has transcended all karmas and resides eternally at the top of the universe. The distinction is therefore crucial for understanding the stages of liberation.

misconceptions.myth: Arihants are less pure than Siddhas because they still have some karmas remaining.
misconceptions.reality: In terms of inner purity of consciousness, Arihants have destroyed all ghātiyā karmas and thus possess flawless knowledge, perception, bliss, and energy. The remaining aghātiyā karmas pertain only to bodily and worldly conditions, not to moral or cognitive impurity. The difference between Arihant and Siddha is not a gradation of spiritual purity but the presence or absence of embodiment and residual non‑destructive karmas.

misconceptions.myth: Siddhas actively intervene in the world, granting boons or changing karmic results for devotees.
misconceptions.reality: Jain philosophy holds that Siddhas are completely beyond action and interaction. Having transcended all karmas, they do not create new karmic bonds, perform acts of will, or intervene in worldly affairs. Devotional focus on Siddhas is directed toward contemplation and aspiration, not expectation of miraculous intervention. Arihants and Tīrthaṅkaras, while embodied, may teach and establish the community, but even they do not override the law of karma for individuals.

misconceptions.myth: Only Tīrthaṅkaras can be Arihants; ordinary kevalins are not Arihants.
misconceptions.reality: In technical doctrinal usage, any soul that has destroyed the ghātiyā karmas and attained omniscience while embodied is an Arihant. Tīrthaṅkaras are a special class of Arihants distinguished by their role as ford‑makers who establish or renew the Jain community and teachings. Other kevalins who do not perform this specific historical and communal function are still Arihants in the sense of being embodied omniscients.
